fact_check_verdict: Publish as an explainer of a USGS statistical forecast pegged to the October 15th Lake Minchumina M5.6. Every figure is read from USGS primary JSON/pages fetched October 16th. NO claim that the model is or is not AI/ML beyond 'a published equation'. NO claim about damage, felt extent, Alaska Earthquake Center, ShakeAlert in Alaska, or any Alaska AI deployment (all unverified, dropped). The AI point is the film's OUR READ, labelled as opinion.

claims.spoken: A magnitude five point six earthquake hit near Lake Minchumina before dawn on October fifteenth.
claims.on_screen: M5.6 · 43 KM NNW OF LAKE MINCHUMINA · OCTOBER 15TH
requires: USGS event aka2026ukynnb, origin 11:07 UTC (3:07 a.m. Alaska time). No damage, felt-extent or injury claim: none was verified.

claims.spoken: a hundred and three people file felt reports
requires: Count as fetched October 16th and may rise. Say 'filed felt reports', never 'felt as far as' any town.

claims.spoken: The U S G S posted odds for it, because it posts them for any quake of magnitude five or bigger outside the lower forty-eight.
claims.on_screen: M5+ OUTSIDE THE LOWER 48 · FORECAST POSTED
requires: Overview text: 'Forecasts are posted for earthquakes of M4+ in the contiguous United States and M5+ in other U.S. states and territories.'

claims.spoken: The forecast came out twelve hours after the shaking.
requires: creationTime 2026-10-15 23:07 UTC vs origin 11:07 UTC, which is 3:07 p.m. Alaska time. Say 'twelve hours later', never 'that evening' or 'that morning'.

claims.spoken: One week out, the chance of another quake of magnitude three or bigger was about forty in a hundred.
requires: Probability 0.3988. A probability, not a prediction.

claims.spoken: For magnitude four or bigger, about seven in a hundred.
For magnitude five or bigger, less than one in a hundred.
And for magnitude six, under one in a thousand.
For magnitude three or bigger, one year is fifty-eight in a hundred.
claims.on_screen: ONE DAY 23 IN 100 · ONE YEAR 58 IN 100 · M3+

claims.spoken: Longer windows get bigger odds, because each window contains the one before it.
claims.on_screen: EACH WINDOW CONTAINS THE ONE BEFORE
requires: Overview: 'each time interval contains the one before (e.g. a one-year forecast includes the first day, first week, and first month) plus additional time.'

claims.spoken: It's a published equation with four dials, named a, b, c and p, from a paper by Reasenberg and Jones.
claims.on_screen: REASENBERG AND JONES · 1989 · FOUR DIALS a b c p
requires: Background: 'We use the statistical model of aftershock rate developed by Reasenberg and Jones (1989, 1994)' and 'a, b, c, and p are model parameters'. Do not call it AI, machine learning or a neural net, and do not state that USGS says it doesn't use ML.

claims.spoken: It starts from how past aftershock sequences behaved, then bends toward this one as the quake keeps going.
claims.on_screen: STARTS FROM PAST SEQUENCES · BENDS TO THIS ONE
requires: Overview: 'We use the behavior of past aftershock sequences to forecast the likelihood of future aftershocks. As an aftershock sequence progresses, our forecast also incorporates information about the behavior of that specific sequence.'

claims.spoken: one aftershock of magnitude three or bigger had been counted
requires: forecast.json observations: M3 count 1, M4 to M7 count 0, at forecast creation.

claims.spoken: Zero to five aftershocks this week
requires: p95minimum 0, p95maximum 5 for the one week M3 bin. Number of aftershocks, a 95 percent range.

claims.spoken: And it says where it breaks. It may perform poorly when big aftershocks set off their own aftershocks.
claims.on_screen: ITS OWN LIMIT · MAY PERFORM POORLY WHEN BIG AFTERSHOCKS TRIGGER MORE
requires: Background: 'It works well for mainshocks followed only by smaller aftershocks, but may perform poorly for sequences with large aftershocks that trigger many of their own aftershocks.' Attribute to USGS.

claims.spoken: Forecasts are updated regularly, and each one carries the time of the next update.
claims.on_screen: NEXT UPDATE TIME PRINTED ON EVERY FORECAST
requires: Overview: 'The time that the current forecast was released, and the planned time of the next forecast update, are included in each forecast.'

claims.spoken: The odds are no idle number, because sometimes the big one comes second. In 2011, a magnitude seven point three quake in Japan came two days before a nine point one.
claims.on_screen: 2011 JAPAN · M7.3 · TWO DAYS LATER · M9.1
requires: Overview: 'the 2011 M9.1 Japan earthquake and tsunami was preceded by a M7.3 foreshock two days before.' Context only, not an Alaska claim.

claims.spoken: The generic version is honest about being unsure, and says its uncertainty is large.
requires: Background: 'the generic aftershock forecasts also tend to have large uncertainty.' Note this forecast is the Bayesian combination of generic and sequence-specific parameters.
